--- title: "Parallel processing in R using Futureverse" subtitle: "A summary of a useR! conference workshop" author: "Ward Langeraert" date: 2026-10-01 editor_options: chunk_output_type: console --- # About this presentation ## Disclaimer - Short summary of the workshop: **"Introduction to Parallel Processing in R using Futureverse - Easier than Ever Before"** - Henrik Bengtsson - useR! conference on 2026-07-06. - These slides are condensed notes from the workshop and do not replace the original workshop materials. - ## Preparation Install packages ```r install.packages("futureverse") install.packages("beepr") ``` \ Make sure everything is up to date ```r futureverse::futureverse_update() #> All futureverse packages up-to-date ``` # About parallel processing ## What is parallel processing? - Execution of **multiple computations** at the same time - Divided into **smaller, independent tasks** - Executed simultaneously by **multiple workers** - Multiple CPU cores - Across multiple machines (distributed computing) --- **Sequential** Task 1 ──────► Task 2 ──────► Task 3 ──────► Task 4 time ► **Parallel** Task 1 ───────────► Task 2 ───────────► Task 3 ───────────► Task 4 ───────────► time ► ## Why do we parallelize code? Parallel processing can be used to: - **Speed** up processing - Finish sooner - **Lower memory** footprint per machine - Handle computations that don't fit on one machine - **Computing where the data lives** - Avoid moving large amounts of data --- > Parallel processing is **not automatically faster**! Parallelization can be slower when: - **Tasks are too small**: per-task overhead (launch, serialize, transfer) exceeds the actual work - **Data is large**: copying inputs and outputs to and from workers dominates - **The bottleneck is not the CPU**: disk-, network-, or memory-bandwidth-bound work does not speed up - **The code is already vectorized**: e.g. `sqrt(xs)` beats any parallel map ## How do we parallelize code? Different types of computing infrastructure: :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} 1. **Personal laptop** - Multiple CPU cores - Typically a single user ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} 2. **Shared powerful computer** - More CPU cores and memory - Multiple users ::: :::: --- Different types of computing infrastructure: :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} 3. **Across many computers** - Computers in the office or in the cloud - Tasks distributed across machines ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} 4. **High-performance computing (HPC) cluster** - Many powerful machines - Multiple users - Job scheduler ::: :::: --- Approach depends on **computational problem** and **available infrastructure**. 1. **Personal laptop** - For many analyses sufficient - Examples: - simulations - bootstrapping - resampling and cross-validation --- Approach depends on **computational problem** and **available infrastructure**. 2. **Shared powerful computer** - INBO has powerful desktop PCs in Brussels and Geraardsbergen - More CPU and memory than a standard laptop - Equipped with a GPU - Suitable for computationally intensive analyses > see also the tutorial ["Geavanceerde analysenoden"](https://ict-intranet.inbo.be/tutorials/geavanceerde_analysenoden/index.html) on ICT intranet --- Approach depends on **computational problem** and **available infrastructure**. 3. **Across many computers** - INBO has cloud infrastructure available through AWS - Work can be distributed across multiple machines - Useful for large numbers of independent or computationally intensive tasks > see also the tutorial ["Geavanceerde analysenoden"](https://ict-intranet.inbo.be/tutorials/geavanceerde_analysenoden/index.html) on ICT intranet --- Approach depends on **computational problem** and **available infrastructure**. 4. **High-performance computing (HPC) cluster** - INBO can make use of HPC infrastructure within the Flemish universities - Many powerful machines and CPU cores - Suitable for large-scale simulations and computationally intensive analyses > see also the tutorial ["Geavanceerde analysenoden"](https://ict-intranet.inbo.be/tutorials/geavanceerde_analysenoden/index.html) on ICT intranet # Parallel processing in R using the Futureverse ## Introducing the Futureverse - Use your existing R code - Scale from your **laptop to HPC** - No need to manually manage: - workers - global variables - parallel random-number generation The same approach works across **Windows, macOS and Linux**.
--- First, let's define a computation of interest: \ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} slow_sum <- function(x) { sum <- 0 for (value in x) { Sys.sleep(1) # one-second slowdown per value sum <- sum + value } sum } ``` ::: --- Verify run time ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tic <- futureverse:::tic toc <- futureverse:::toc ``` ::: \ Let's take the sum of 1, 2, 3 (slowly!) ```r tic() toc(slow_sum(1:3)) # or: slow_sum(1:3) |> toc() ``` ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` [0 secs] ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` [3 secs] +3.03 secs : slow_sum(1:3) ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 6 ``` ::: ::: ## Working with futures - A **future**: an abstraction for a value that will be available later - A **value**: the result of an evaluated expression :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="35%"} An **R assignment**: ```r v <- expr ``` ::: ::: {.column width="10%"} ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} A **future-value assignment**: ```r f <- future(expr) v <- value(f) ``` ::: :::: --- Your turn: `future()` and `value()` \ :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="32%"} - Verify result - Verify run time ::: ::: {.column width="68%"} ```r library(future) plan(multisession) x <- 1:10 fa <- future(slow_sum(x[1:5])) fb <- future(slow_sum(x[6:10])) y <- value(fa) + value(fb) ``` ::: :::: --- :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="32%"} **Sequential** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- 1:10 ``` ::: \ ```r tic() slow_sum(x) toc() ``` ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` [0 secs] ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 55 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` [10.1 secs] ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="3%"} ::: ::: {.column width="65%"} **Parallel** ```r library(future) plan(multisession) tic() fa <- future(slow_sum(x[1:5])) fb <- future(slow_sum(x[6:10])) value(fa) + value(fb) toc() ``` ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` [0 secs] ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 55 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` [5.1 secs] ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Apply the same function over and over Slow square root ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} slow_sqrt <- function(x) { Sys.sleep(0.5) # half-second delay per item sqrt(x) } ``` ::: :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="47%"} Base R: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} xs <- as.list(1:5) ys <- xs |> lapply(slow_sqrt) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="53%"} tidyverse: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(purrr) xs <- as.list(1:5) ys <- map(xs, slow_sqrt) ``` ::: ::: :::: --- **Task:** Create a function `ys <- parallel_map(xs, slow_sqrt)` :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="67%"} Combine the idea of: ```r f <- future(slow_sqrt(x)) v <- value(f) ``` with: ```r ys <- list() for (i in seq_along(xs)) { ys[[i]] <- slow_sqrt(xs[[i]]) } ``` ::: ::: {.column width="3%"} ::: ::: {.column width="30%"} \ > Hint: You need two for-loops, one for `future()` and one for `value()` ::: :::: --- ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} parallel_map <- function(.x, .f) { # Create futures fs <- vector(mode = "list", length = length(.x)) for (i in seq_along(.x)) { fs[[i]] <- future::future(.f(.x[[i]])) } # Collect values ys <- vector(mode = "list", length = length(.x)) for (i in seq_along(.x)) { ys[[i]] <- future::value(fs[[i]]) } return(ys) } ``` ::: --- :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **Sequential** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(123) xs <- runif(30) ``` ::: \ ```r tic() ys_seq <- xs |> purrr::map(slow_sqrt) toc() ``` ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` [0 secs] ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` [15.2 secs] ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Parallel** ```r library(future) plan(multisession, workers = 4) tic() ys_par <- xs |> parallel_map(slow_sqrt) toc() ``` ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` [0 secs] ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` [4.7 secs] ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: --- ## Let’s simplify our lives with futurize - `futurize()` is new since January 2026 - Rewrites expression into equivalent Futureverse call, then evaluates ```r ys <- lapply(xs, slow_sqrt) # {base} ys <- lapply(xs, slow_sqrt) |> futurize() # {futurize} ``` \ ```r ys <- map(xs, slow_sqrt) # {base} ys <- map(xs, slow_sqrt) |> futurize() # {futurize} ```
--- Popular statistics packages support `futurize()` \ ```r # Bootstrap ({boot}) boot::boot(data, statistic, R = 1000) |> futurize() # Cross-validation ({glmnet}) glmnet::cv.glmnet(x, y) |> futurize() # Model tuning ({caret}) caret::train(y ~ ., data = d, method = "rf") |> futurize() # Additive models ({mgcv}) mgcv::bam(y ~ s(x1) + s(x2), data = d) |> futurize() # Mixed-model bootstrap ({lme4}) lme4::bootMer(fit, statistic, nsim = 1000) |> futurize() ``` --- The code stays the same --> only the `plan()` changes \ **On your machine** ```r plan(sequential) # sequential (default) plan(multisession, workers = 4) # parallel ``` \ Or use alternative local back ends such as **future.mirai** and **future.callr** ```r plan(future.mirai::mirai_multisession) ``` --- **Other machines** Distributed across local or remote computers ```r plan(cluster, workers = c("n1", "m2.uni.edu", "vm.cloud.org")) ``` \ **HPC clusters** Run futures through an HPC job scheduler ```r plan(future.batchtools::batchtools_slurm) ``` # Progress reporting ## Measure running times with `progressify()` - Similar method for progress reporting - The code stays the same --> only the `handlers()` change ```r library(progressify) handlers(global = TRUE) # Must be enabled manually! ys <- lapply(1:10, slow_sqrt) |> progressify() ``` `|============================= | 80%`
--- 🔊 \ ```r library(progressify) handlers("cli", "beepr", global = TRUE) ys <- lapply(1:10, slow_sqrt) |> progressify() ``` `■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■■ 80% | ETA: 1s` with ♫♪♬♫ … ♬♫ ## Parallelize and report - Combine `progressify()` and `futurize()` ```r library(futurize) library(progressify) plan(multisession, workers = 4) handlers("cli", global = TRUE) ys <- lapply(1:10, slow_sqrt) |> progressify() |> futurize() ``` # More on parallelization ## Things we haven’t talked about - Message, warning and error handling - Random number generation in parallel processing - Not everything can travel to a worker (e.g. database connections) - Nested parallelization, efficient memory handling, resource management ... > More info in the [original tutorial](https://henrikbengtsson.github.io/futureverse-tutorial-user2026/#/) or on [www.futureverse.org](https://www.futureverse.org/)

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
